# Datalog in a box

A Field document is a graph. Boxes have parents and children, they nest, they carry properties,
and the questions you end up asking about one are recursive: what runs downstream of this, what
does nothing feed into, which two boxes both write the same property. `graphPaths`
([Querying Object Graphs](graph_query.md)) can address a slot by pattern, but it cannot follow an
edge and then follow it again.

`afield.data.query.datalog` can. It is a small deductive database: you state facts, you write rules that
derive more facts from them, and the engine runs the rules to exhaustion. Recursion is the normal
case rather than a special one, so transitive closure is two lines. Facts can come from Datalog
text, from Kotlin collections, or from the document you have open.

## Facts, rules, and a question

A fact is a row. A rule reads `head :- body`, which you can say out loud as *head if body*.
Capitalised names are variables; lowercase names are constants, so `imports(app, ui)` and
`imports("app", "ui")` are the same fact.

<!--
FIELD_TEST

timeoutSec: 90
waitSec: 2.0
expect:
  outputContains:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/modules.png" alt="the Kotlin box in the editor with two inline output strips wedged between its lines: one under the first println reading 'app needs log, store, ui, util', one under the last carrying 'modules that need log: 4' and 'does app need log? true'. Inside the triple-quoted string the #datalog marker is gold, rule heads are blue and the variables A, B and C are orange" capture="editor" outputs="inline" wait="4" padding="10" timeout="180" embed=true name="datalog-modules" w="900" h="420"}
:::static
val d = Datalog()
d.add("""
    #datalog
    % which module pulls in which
    imports(app, ui).    imports(app, store).
    imports(ui, util).   imports(store, util).  imports(util, log).

    needs(A, B) :- imports(A, B).
    needs(A, C) :- needs(A, B), imports(B, C).
""")

println("app needs " + d.query("needs(app, X)").column("X").joinToString(", "))
println("does app need log? " + d.ask("needs(app, log)"))
println("modules that need log: " + d.query("needs(A, log)").size)
```

Answers land beside the line that asked: edit a rule, run, read. Two rules for `needs`, read as
alternatives: `app` needs whatever it imports, and it needs whatever *that* needs. Nothing says how
far to follow the chain, and nothing has to.

The `#datalog` on the first line is a marker the editor looks for; the parser ignores it. Leave it
out and the program still runs. Put it in and the region lights up, which the last section covers.

## The answer is a fixpoint

`query` runs one goal. `solve` hands back the whole model: every relation, with every fact the
rules can derive.

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.fixpoint
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, tohtml]
timeoutSec: 60
waitSec: 1.5
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "facts in 2 relations"
    - "path"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/fixpoint.png" alt="the main output channel: a heading reading '16 facts in 2 relations' over a three-column table of relation, arity and rows, listing edge at arity 2 with 4 rows and path at arity 2 with 12" wait="1.5" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="main" capture="box" embed=true name="datalog-fixpoint" w="760" h="260"}
:::static
val d = Datalog()
d.add("""
    #datalog
    edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, d). edge(d, b).
    path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).
    path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), edge(Y, Z).
""")

display("main", d.solve())
```

Four stated edges produce twelve paths. The cycle `b → c → d → b` makes those three nodes mutually
reachable, including each from itself. The rules still stop: they can only combine values that are
already there, so after a few rounds there is nothing new to add.

## Why a fact is there

`why` shows how a fact was derived: which rules fired, and which stated facts they started from.

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.why
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, tohtml]
timeoutSec: 60
waitSec: 1.5
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "why path(a, d)"
    - "edge(c, d)"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/why.png" alt="a derivation tree headed 'why path(a, d)', indented by arrow glyphs: path(a, d) from the recursive clause, then path(a, c) from the same clause, then path(a, b) from the base clause, and at the leaves edge(a, b), edge(b, c) and edge(c, d), each tagged [fact]. Every interior node carries the rule that fired it in brackets" wait="1.5" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="main" capture="box" embed=true name="datalog-why" w="760" h="260"}
:::static
val d = Datalog()
d.add("""
    #datalog
    edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, d). edge(d, b).
    path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).
    path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), edge(Y, Z).
""")

display("main", d.why("path(a, d)"))
```

Each line names the rule that produced it, and the leaves are facts you stated. Cycles are fine:
`path(a, a)` in the graph above gets a finite proof too.

A proof runs through an aggregate as well. A fact derived through `count` or `sum` lists the rows
that contributed to it and the arithmetic that combined them:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
payroll(sales, 300)   [payroll(D, S) :- dept(D), S = sum P : { emp(_1, D, P) }]
    dept(sales)   [fact]
    S = sum P : { emp(_1, sales, P) }   [aggregate: sum over 2 tuples = 300]
        emp(ada, sales, 100)   [fact; contributes P = 100]
        emp(bob, sales, 200)   [fact; contributes P = 200]
```

`min` and `max` label the tuple that was the extreme, and keep the rest of the group in the proof
too, because "nothing bigger exists" is half of what the answer means. A group is capped at 24 lines
of display; the value is always computed over the whole of it. A negated body literal appears as its
own step, since "no such fact" is often the reason a rule fired.

## Why one is not

An empty result gives no reason, so `whyNot` runs the query one goal at a time and names the goal
where the answers ran out.

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
whynot cell(C, V), V > 5, colour(C, red)   no answers
     1  cell(C, V)      3 answers
     2  V > 5           1 answer
     3  colour(C, red)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
    a binding that got this far: C = a3, V = 10
```

Ask about a single derived fact and it does the same walk once per rule that could have produced it,
with the head's constants filled in, and puts the attempt that got furthest first:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
whynot path(a, e)   not in the model; 2 rule(s) could have produced it
  via path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), edge(Y, Z)
       1  path(a, Y)  3 answers
       2  edge(Y, e)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
      a binding that got this far: Y = b
  via path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y)
       1  edge(a, e)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
```

`whyNot` tells apart three causes that look the same in an empty result: a goal with no matching
rows, a predicate nothing defines, and a test written before the goal that binds its variable. The
last is reported as "not evaluable this early", because the fix is to reorder the rule rather than
to look for missing data.

## Facts from Kotlin objects

`facts` takes Kotlin objects and a projection, so the rules can run over whatever you already have
in the box. Negation and aggregation are both available, with the usual condition: they need the
relations they read to be finished first, so a rule may not negate or aggregate over something that
depends on itself. The engine checks and says so by name if you try.

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.takes
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, tohtml]
timeoutSec: 60
waitSec: 1.5
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "footage(S, Total, Best)"
    - "insert"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/takes.png" alt="two stacked output channels. The main one, headed '?- footage(S, Total, Best) (3 rows)', tabulates close 41 4, insert 19 2 and wide 80 5: one row per shot, not per take. The reshoot channel below it, headed '?- reshoot(S) (1 row)', holds the single answer insert" wait="1.5" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="main" capture="box" embed=true name="datalog-takes" w="760" h="330"}
:::static
data class Take(val clip: String, val shot: String, val seconds: Int, val rating: Int)

val takes = [
    Take("a017", "wide",   42, 5), Take("a018", "wide",   38, 2),
    Take("a021", "close",  19, 4), Take("a022", "close",  22, 3),
    Take("a030", "insert",  8, 2), Take("a031", "insert", 11, 1),
]

val d = Datalog()
d.facts("take", takes) { [it.clip, it.shot, it.seconds, it.rating] }
d.facts("shot", [["wide"], ["close"], ["insert"]])
d.add("""
    #datalog
    covered(S) :- take(_, S, _, R), R >= 4.
    reshoot(S) :- shot(S), !covered(S).
    footage(S, Total, Best) :- shot(S),
        Total = sum Sec : { take(_, S, Sec, _) },
        Best  = max R   : { take(_, S, _, R) }.
""")

display("main", d.query("footage(S, Total, Best)"))
display("reshoot", d.query("reshoot(S)"))
```

An aggregate groups by whichever of its variables the enclosing rule has already bound. `shot(S)`
binds `S` before the aggregate runs, so `sum Sec : { take(_, S, Sec, _) }` totals one shot at a
time. Take `shot(S)` out and you get one number for the whole table.

`_` is a hole, and each one is separate: `take(_, S, Sec, _)` means *some* take of this shot, not a
take whose clip and rating are equal. Under `!` a hole is existential, so `!covered(S)` and
`!child(_, X)` both mean "no row matches".

## The document is a database

`Box.datalog(...)` loads the graph you are looking at. Boxes, names, edges, nesting, frames and
scalar properties all arrive as relations:

Which makes the recursive questions about a document short. Here the graph is built in the box so
the answer is reproducible, but `thisBox.datalog(program)` runs the identical rules against the
document you have open:

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.document
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, tohtml]
timeoutSec: 60
waitSec: 1.5
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "downstream(loader, X)"
    - "shader"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/document.png" alt="two output channels over the six-box toy document. The main one, '?- downstream(loader, X), name(X, N) (3 rows)', lists draw, mesh and shader, draw among them although it hangs two edges below loader. The leaves channel, '?- leaf(X), name(X, N) (3 rows)', lists draw, notes and shader" wait="1.5" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="main" capture="box" embed=true name="datalog-document" w="760" h="380"}
:::static
fun boxNamed(id: String, name: String, parent: Box?): Box {
    val b = Box(id)
    b.name = name
    if (parent != null) { parent.children.add(b); b.parents.add(parent) }
    return b
}

val root   = boxNamed("root", "document", null)
val loader = boxNamed("loader", "loader", root)
val mesh   = boxNamed("mesh", "mesh", loader)
val shader = boxNamed("shader", "shader", loader)
val draw   = boxNamed("draw", "draw", mesh)
val notes  = boxNamed("notes", "notes", root)

val d = Datalog()
d.addBoxGraph(root)
d.add("""
    #datalog
    downstream(A, B) :- child(A, B).
    downstream(A, C) :- downstream(A, B), child(B, C).
    leaf(X) :- box(X), !child(X, _).
""")

display("main", d.query("downstream(loader, X), name(X, N)"))
display("leaves", d.query("leaf(X), name(X, N)"))
```

The graph is read once, as a snapshot, so an answer describes the document as it was when you
asked. Build a new `Datalog` to refresh it.

## Any object graph

`addBoxGraph` knows about boxes. For any other Kotlin object, `addObjectGraph` walks it the way
[`graphPaths`](graph_query.md) does and turns every slot it visits into facts. A `graphPaths`
pattern can address slots but cannot follow an edge repeatedly, or notice that two paths lead to
the same object; Datalog supplies both.

`addObjectGraph` gives `slot`, `link`, `segment`, `depth`, `at`, `value`, `type` and `writable`;
`dlObjectGraphRules` adds `alias`, `reaches`, `unreached` and `leaf` on top. In `at(Path, ObjectId)`
every non-scalar value gets a number by identity, so two paths that reach the same object share a
number, and `alias` is `at` joined with itself:

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.object_graph
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, graphquery, tohtml]
timeoutSec: 90
waitSec: 2.0
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "alias(A, B)"
    - "spare"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/object_graph.png" alt="two output channels. The main one, '?- alias(A, B) (2 rows)', pairs carrier with spare and spare with carrier: the two names the walk found for one oscillator. The settable channel, '?- reaches(carrier, P), writable(P) (2 rows)', lists the paths carrier/freq and carrier/gain" wait="1.5" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="main" capture="box" embed=true name="datalog-object-graph" w="760" h="420"}
:::static
class Osc(var freq: Float, var gain: Float, val label: String)
class Rig(val carrier: Osc, val modulator: Osc, val spare: Osc, var title: String)

// carrier and spare are one oscillator under two names. Nothing in the type says so.
val shared = Osc(220f, 0.8f, "shared")
val rig = Rig(shared, Osc(440f, 0.2f, "mod"), shared, "rig")

val d = Datalog()
d.addObjectGraph(rig)
d.add(dlObjectGraphRules)

display("main", d.query("alias(A, B)"))
display("settable", d.query("reaches(\"carrier\", P), writable(P)"))
```

`alias` finds the two names for one oscillator. It compares identity, not equality, so two separate
oscillators with the same settings would not match.

The second answer lists every settable slot anywhere below `carrier`, which takes the recursive
step a `graphPaths` pattern cannot express.

Narrow the walk with a `graphPaths` pattern: `addObjectGraph(rig, "carrier/*")` loads one level,
and a literal prefix is much cheaper than `**`, which walks everything.

For a document, use `addBoxGraph` anyway: its `child`, `nested`, `frame` and `prop` relations are
what you want to ask about, where a walk of a `Box` object turns up every internal field it has.

## Drawing what it derived

Query results are rows of ordinary values, so anything that eats values can eat them. Below, the
rules separate stated edges from the ones that follow, and the drawing gives each set a weight:

<!--
FIELD_TEST
id: docs.datalog.reachability_figure
runner: backdoor-box
tags: [docs, datalog, fline]
timeoutSec: 90
waitSec: 1.5
expect:
  outputContains:
    - "8 stated edges, 34 implied by them"
-->
```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/datalog/reachability.png" alt="seven yellow diamond nodes numbered 0 to 6 around an ellipse. Eight thick yellow lines are the stated edges, the ring 0-1-2-3-4 back to 0, plus the branch 1-5-6 rejoining at 2. Behind them a dense haze of thin blue-grey lines joins almost every other pair of nodes: the implied edges, outnumbering the stated ones four to one" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" embed=true name="datalog-reachability" w="760" h="430"}
:::static
val links = [0 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 0, 1 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 2]

val d = Datalog()
d.facts("edge", links.map { [it.first, it.second] })
d.add("""
    #datalog
    path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).
    path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), edge(Y, Z).
    implied(X, Y) :- path(X, Y), !edge(X, Y), X != Y.
""")

val n = 7
fun at(i: Int): Vec2 {
    val a = i * 2.0 * PI / n - PI / 2
    return vec(340.0 + 300.0 * cos(a), 170.0 + 135.0 * sin(a))
}
fun link(a: Int, b: Int, c: Vec4, t: Double) = fline {
    val p = at(a); val q = at(b)
    moveTo(p.x, p.y)
    lineTo(q.x, q.y)
    color = c
    thickness = t
}
fun dot(i: Int) = fline {
    val p = at(i); val r = 5.0
    moveTo(p.x - r, p.y); lineTo(p.x, p.y - r); lineTo(p.x + r, p.y); lineTo(p.x, p.y + r)
    close()
    filled = true
    color = vec(0.98, 0.86, 0.30, 1.0)
}
// Node numbers, set just outside the ring so an edge never runs through one. Glyphs move with
// FLine.transform, which carries the cubic handles; nudging a node's point alone smears the letter.
fun label(i: Int): List<FLine> = runCatching {
    val a = i * 2.0 * PI / n - PI / 2
    val p = at(i)
    val layout = layoutText("$i", typeface("Monospaced", 22.0))
    val dx = p.x + 26.0 * cos(a) - layout.advanceWidth / 2.0
    val dy = p.y + 26.0 * sin(a) + 8.0
    layout.toFLines(color = vec(0.72, 0.78, 0.86, 1.0), thickness = 0.0, filled = true, stroked = false)
        .map { line -> line.transform { q -> vec(q.x + dx, q.y + dy, q.z) } }
}.getOrElse { emptyList() }

val implied = d.query("implied(X, Y)").rows
    .map { link((it[0] as Long).toInt(), (it[1] as Long).toInt(), vec(0.45, 0.70, 0.98, 0.20), 1.0) }
val direct = links.map { link(it.first, it.second, vec(0.98, 0.86, 0.30, 1.0), 2.0) }

println("${links.size} stated edges, ${implied.size} implied by them")
val labels = (0 until n).flatMap { label(it) }
lines(implied + direct + (0 until n).map { dot(it) } + labels, w = 700.0, h = 350.0, fitToSize = true)
```

Eight edges, thirty-four consequences. The faint lines are what `implied` derived, and the rule
that made them is the third line of the program. Its `X != Y` drops self-reachability, which the
cycle `0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 0` would otherwise contribute for every node on it.

## A box that is Datalog

Set a box's main language to Datalog (`Set Main Language: Datalog` in the command palette) and its
children hold programs instead of Kotlin. A Datalog box accumulates: running a fragment merges it
into that box's program and prints what the fragment asked for, so you can write a rule, run it,
write a query underneath, and run just that line. Re-running the whole box is safe, because
identical rules are merged rather than appended.

A bare non-ground atom on its own is read as a question, so `over(C).` asks rather than failing as
a fact with a variable in it. Lines beginning with `#` are session commands.

No Kotlin at all in one of these. The box below is a Datalog box, and this is its whole contents:

Below the last line an inline output strip repeats the goal and gives a one-column table whose single answer is a3" capture="editor" outputs="inline" wait="4" wait-output=true wait-output-kind="all" padding="10" timeout="240" embed=true name="datalog-box" w="900" h="360"}
:::static
% a spreadsheet's worth of cells, and one rule about them
cell(a1, 3). cell(a2, 4). cell(a3, 10).

?- over(C).

Run a `#why` next to it and the box answers with the derivation rather than the row:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=datalog screenshot="assets/datalog/box_why.png" capture="editor" outputs="inline" wait="4" wait-output=true wait-output-kind="all" padding="10" timeout="240" name="datalog-box-why" w="900" h="300" embed=true}

The session commands are `#help`, `#boxes` (load the live document into the base relations),
`#relations`, `#facts <relation>`, `#program`, `#why <goal>`, `#whynot <goal>` and `#reset`. A `#why`
about a fact that is not there points you at `#whynot`, which is where you wanted to be.

## The editor knows the language

A Kotlin string whose first line is `#datalog` is an embedded region, in the same way `#stacksl`
and `#petri` regions work ([Language Extensions](language_extensions.md)). Rule heads are coloured
differently from the same predicate used in a body, variables differently from constants, and
hovering a predicate reports its arity and how many clauses define it. Completion offers the
program's own predicates first, then the builtins and the box-graph relations.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="editor" screenshot="assets/datalog/region.png" alt="eleven lines of Kotlin in the editor, the middle eight of them inside a triple-quoted string that opens with a gold #datalog. Within the region the rule heads needs, busy and orphan are blue while the same imports predicate is blue where it heads a fact and plain white inside a rule body; variables are orange, constants white, and the aggregate keyword count is violet" wait="0" timeout="120" embed=true hidden=true name="datalog-region"}

ui.openEditor(id)
ui.pause(700)
// Set the model rather than typing it: the region only exists once its closing triple quote does,
// and a half-typed literal has nothing to highlight.
ui.eval(
    "var q = String.fromCharCode(34).repeat(3);" +
    "var code = ['val d = Datalog()', 'd.add(' + q, '#datalog'," +
    " '% which module pulls in which', 'imports(app, ui).  imports(ui, util).'," +
    " 'needs(A, B) :- imports(A, B).', 'needs(A, C) :- needs(A, B), imports(B, C).'," +
    " 'busy(M, N) :- imports(M, _), N = count : { needs(M, _) }.'," +
    " 'orphan(M) :- imports(_, M), !imports(M, _).', q + ')'," +
    " 'display(' + q.slice(0,1) + 'main' + q.slice(0,1) + ', d.query(' + q.slice(0,1) + 'needs(app, X)' + q.slice(0,1) + '))'].join('\\n');" +
    "window.globalEditor.getModel().setValue(code); return 'set';"
)
ui.pause(1500)
```

Diagnostics inside a region are lexical only: unbalanced brackets, an unterminated string, a clause
with no `.`. The rules in "What it refuses" below are checked when the program runs.

Rest the cursor on a statement and the note beside it answers from the box's model: a rule says how
many facts its body derives there and draws them as a table, a query shows its answers, and a fact says
whether it is in the model and which rules read its relation. A rule edited since it last ran is
reported as not in the model, and no directive is ever run for a note — see
[Line notes](language_extensions.md#line-notes).

## Reference

**Syntax.** `%` and `//` start a line comment, `/* */` a block. A clause ends with `.`. A variable
starts with a capital letter or `_`; everything else lowercase is a constant string. Numbers,
`"strings"`, `true`, `false` and `null` are literals. `!goal` or `not goal` negates. `?- goal.`
records a query.

**Arithmetic.** `+ - * /`, `mod`, `div`, and comparisons `= != < <= > >=`. `X = expr` binds `X`
when nothing has bound it yet and compares when something has. `+` concatenates if either side is a
string. Every integral number is stored as a `Long`, including a computed `4.0 / 2.0`, so
arithmetic results join with stated facts.

**Functions.** `abs sign sqrt floor ceil round pow exp log sin cos tan atan2 hypot min max len
upper lower trim cat substr indexOf contains startsWith endsWith split num str int not`. A call to
one of these on its own is a test, so `contains(N, "shader")` filters.

**Aggregates.** `count sum min max mean collect`, written `X = op Expr : { body }` (`count` takes
no expression). `min`, `max` and `mean` of an empty group have no value, so the rule does not fire
for that group; `count` and `sum` give 0. The target has to be a variable nothing has bound yet, so
"the maximum, and who earned it" is two rules rather than one.

**Explaining.** `why(goal)` returns a derivation tree, through aggregates and negation as well as
rules, or null when the fact is not in the model. `whyNot(goal)` returns the narrowing walk instead.
Both implement `ToHTML`, so `display(…)` of either from a Kotlin box draws an indented table; the
`#why` and `#whynot` directives inside a Datalog box print `render()`'s plain text instead.

**What it refuses.** A rule whose head has a variable the body never binds. A negated goal whose
variables are bound nowhere else. A predicate used at two different arities. Negation or
aggregation inside a recursive cycle, which it reports with the cycle named rather than picking an
evaluation order.

# Datalog in a box

A Field document is a graph. Boxes have parents and children, they nest, they carry properties,
and the questions you end up asking about one are recursive: what runs downstream of this, what
does nothing feed into, which two boxes both write the same property. `graphPaths`
([Querying Object Graphs](graph_query.md)) can address a slot by pattern, but it cannot follow an
edge and then follow it again.

`afield.data.query.datalog` can. It is a small deductive database: you state facts, you write rules that
derive more facts from them, and the engine runs the rules to exhaustion. Recursion is the normal
case rather than a special one, so transitive closure is two lines. Facts can come from Datalog
text, from Kotlin collections, or from the document you have open.

## Facts, rules, and a question

A fact is a row. A rule reads `head :- body`, which you can say out loud as *head if body*.
Capitalised names are variables; lowercase names are constants, so `imports(app, ui)` and
`imports("app", "ui")` are the same fact.

## Why one is not

An empty result gives no reason, so `whyNot` runs the query one goal at a time and names the goal
where the answers ran out.

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
whynot cell(C, V), V > 5, colour(C, red)   no answers
     1  cell(C, V)      3 answers
     2  V > 5           1 answer
     3  colour(C, red)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
    a binding that got this far: C = a3, V = 10
```

Ask about a single derived fact and it does the same walk once per rule that could have produced it,
with the head's constants filled in, and puts the attempt that got furthest first:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
whynot path(a, e)   not in the model; 2 rule(s) could have produced it
  via path(X, Z) :- path(X, Y), edge(Y, Z)
       1  path(a, Y)  3 answers
       2  edge(Y, e)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
      a binding that got this far: Y = b
  via path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y)
       1  edge(a, e)  0 answers   <- nothing survives here
```

`whyNot` tells apart three causes that look the same in an empty result: a goal with no matching
rows, a predicate nothing defines, and a test written before the goal that binds its variable. The
last is reported as "not evaluable this early", because the fix is to reorder the rule rather than
to look for missing data.

## Reference

**Syntax.** `%` and `//` start a line comment, `/* */` a block. A clause ends with `.`. A variable
starts with a capital letter or `_`; everything else lowercase is a constant string. Numbers,
`"strings"`, `true`, `false` and `null` are literals. `!goal` or `not goal` negates. `?- goal.`
records a query.

**Arithmetic.** `+ - * /`, `mod`, `div`, and comparisons `= != < <= > >=`. `X = expr` binds `X`
when nothing has bound it yet and compares when something has. `+` concatenates if either side is a
string. Every integral number is stored as a `Long`, including a computed `4.0 / 2.0`, so
arithmetic results join with stated facts.

**Functions.** `abs sign sqrt floor ceil round pow exp log sin cos tan atan2 hypot min max len
upper lower trim cat substr indexOf contains startsWith endsWith split num str int not`. A call to
one of these on its own is a test, so `contains(N, "shader")` filters.

**Aggregates.** `count sum min max mean collect`, written `X = op Expr : { body }` (`count` takes
no expression). `min`, `max` and `mean` of an empty group have no value, so the rule does not fire
for that group; `count` and `sum` give 0. The target has to be a variable nothing has bound yet, so
"the maximum, and who earned it" is two rules rather than one.

**Explaining.** `why(goal)` returns a derivation tree, through aggregates and negation as well as
rules, or null when the fact is not in the model. `whyNot(goal)` returns the narrowing walk instead.
Both implement `ToHTML`, so `display(…)` of either from a Kotlin box draws an indented table; the
`#why` and `#whynot` directives inside a Datalog box print `render()`'s plain text instead.

**What it refuses.** A rule whose head has a variable the body never binds. A negated goal whose
variables are bound nowhere else. A predicate used at two different arities. Negation or
aggregation inside a recursive cycle, which it reports with the cycle named rather than picking an
evaluation order.

# Filling a solid: tetrahedral meshing with TetGen [Manifold](manifold.md) gives Field surfaces that are guaranteed closed. A closed surface is a boundary: it says where the part stops. It says nothing about the inside, and every question worth asking about a part — how much does it deflect, where does it get hot, where does it crack — is a question about the inside. A tetrahedral mesh is the inside, written down. [TetGen](https://wias-berlin.de/software/tetgen/) takes the closed triangle surface and fills the volume it bounds with tetrahedra whose faces match that surface exactly. In a box, `Tetgen.tetrahedralize` takes a closed `TriMesh` and returns a `TetMesh`. This one fills an L-shaped part built with Manifold: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} import afield.geometry.solid.manifold.* import afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen.* val part = Solid.cube(80.0, 40.0, 15.0) + Solid.cube(15.0, 40.0, 70.0) // an L, 30 triangles val mesh = Tetgen.tetrahedralize(part.toTriMesh(), targetEdgeLength = 5.0) mesh.nodeCount // 2287 mesh.cellCount // 10093 mesh.volume() // 81000.00000000007, against Manifold's exact 81000.0 ``` Every public declaration carries KDoc, browsable on the [Simulation](reference/simulation.md) reference page: start from [`Tetgen`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetgen), [`TetMesh`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetmesh) and [`TetgenLibrary`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetgenlibrary). ## What a tetrahedral mesh is for Field's Kratos bridge solves conduction and flow on a fixed background grid: it samples a signed distance function onto the grid and cuts the body out of it. That is an *embedded* formulation, and it is the cheaper thing to do. Structural mechanics in Kratos cannot work that way, because Kratos has no immersed structural element, so `structural.bodyFitted` needs a mesh whose boundary really is the part's surface. There is a second reason. Sampling a distance function onto grid nodes rounds off a sharp edge before the mesher ever sees it, and refining the grid only makes the rounded radius smaller. Structural stress concentrates at exactly those edges. [The sharp edge](#the-sharp-edge) below shows both. ## The first mesh A tetrahedral mesh is awkward to look at, which is a real obstacle to trusting one. Render it naively and you see the boundary — the surface you already had — while everything the mesher actually did stays hidden. `afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen` has three answers, and the figure below is all three: `boundary()` for the skin, `filtered()` with a half-space test for a cutaway, and `toTriMesh(shrink = …)` for the view where each element stands slightly apart from its neighbours. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/tetgen/cutaway.png" alt="three views of the same bent bracket, side by side. Bending needs strain to vary across a section, tension on one face and compression on the other, so 4-node elements resist it and come out far too stiff (this is called locking). # Filling a solid: tetrahedral meshing with TetGen [Manifold](manifold.md) gives Field surfaces that are guaranteed closed. A closed surface is a boundary: it says where the part stops. It says nothing about the inside, and every question worth asking about a part — how much does it deflect, where does it get hot, where does it crack — is a question about the inside. A tetrahedral mesh is the inside, written down. [TetGen](https://wias-berlin.de/software/tetgen/) takes the closed triangle surface and fills the volume it bounds with tetrahedra whose faces match that surface exactly. In a box, `Tetgen.tetrahedralize` takes a closed `TriMesh` and returns a `TetMesh`. This one fills an L-shaped part built with Manifold: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} import afield.geometry.solid.manifold.* import afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen.* val part = Solid.cube(80.0, 40.0, 15.0) + Solid.cube(15.0, 40.0, 70.0) // an L, 30 triangles val mesh = Tetgen.tetrahedralize(part.toTriMesh(), targetEdgeLength = 5.0) mesh.nodeCount // 2287 mesh.cellCount // 10093 mesh.volume() // 81000.00000000007, against Manifold's exact 81000.0 ``` Every public declaration carries KDoc, browsable on the [Simulation](reference/simulation.md) reference page: start from [`Tetgen`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetgen), [`TetMesh`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetmesh) and [`TetgenLibrary`](reference/simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetgenlibrary). ## What a tetrahedral mesh is for Field's Kratos bridge solves conduction and flow on a fixed background grid: it samples a signed distance function onto the grid and cuts the body out of it. That is an *embedded* formulation, and it is the cheaper thing to do. Structural mechanics in Kratos cannot work that way, because Kratos has no immersed structural element, so `structural.bodyFitted` needs a mesh whose boundary really is the part's surface. There is a second reason. Sampling a distance function onto grid nodes rounds off a sharp edge before the mesher ever sees it, and refining the grid only makes the rounded radius smaller. Structural stress concentrates at exactly those edges. [The sharp edge](#the-sharp-edge) below shows both. ## The first mesh A tetrahedral mesh is awkward to look at, which is a real obstacle to trusting one. Render it naively and you see the boundary — the surface you already had — while everything the mesher actually did stays hidden. `afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen` has three answers, and the figure below is all three: `boundary()` for the skin, `filtered()` with a half-space test for a cutaway, and `toTriMesh(shrink = …)` for the view where each element stands slightly apart from its neighbours. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/tetgen/cutaway.png" alt="three views of the same bent bracket, side by side. The 4-node tetrahedron is a constant-strain element: its corners carry a linear displacement field, so strain has one value across the whole element. Bending needs strain to vary across a section, tension on one face and compression on the other, so 4-node elements resist it and come out far too stiff (this is called locking). # Keyframes: capturing, persisting and replaying live state

*Every `keyframer.kt` declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference:
[`keyframer.kt`](reference/graphics.md#keyframer-kt). The two supporting types the examples lean on,
`afield.graphics.vulkan.buffers.Structure` and `afield.graphics.vulkan.util.CameraPose`, are not: they live in
Field 4, which the [reference](reference/index.md) leaves to
[Field 4 Graphics](afield_four_graphics.md).*

Live coding has a specific kind of loss built into it. You push sliders around for twenty minutes,
arrive somewhere good, and then the thing you arrived at exists only as the current contents of a
running process. Reload the shader and it is gone. Close the document and it is gone. Try to
reproduce it tomorrow from memory and you get something that is *nearly* it, which is worse.

`keyframer.kt` is the answer to that: a `KeyframeScope` is a set of named live targets, `capture()`
reads all of them into a `Key`, and invoking that `Key` writes them all back. Once a look is a
`Key`, it is an ordinary value: you can diff it against another one, blend between them, write it
to disk with a version history, or turn it into Kotlin source you can paste into a box and commit.

The blending half of this (numbers and vectors easing while *code* steps discretely) has a worked
example over on
[Values over time](interpolants_examples.md#keyframes-morphing-a-whole-parameter-state-including-code).
This page is the rest of it: what a scope can watch, why a camera move is a screw motion, how saving
works and what survives it, and how a captured look becomes source.

Almost everything below runs on the CPU, without a renderer.

??? aside "Why most of this page needs no GPU"
    `Structure` is constructible bare
(`Structure.kt:112#open class Structure(`) and its `bind`/`bindings` are plain map operations
    (`Structure.kt:176#fun bind(property: String, value: Function0<*>) {`, `Structure.kt:136#val bindings: MutableMap<String, Function0<*>> = root?.bindings`), so a keyframe scope can be exercised, and tested,
    without a GPU. The exception is
    [the GPU still](#the-same-thing-driving-a-live-gpu-uniform), which is a real Vulkan render, and the
    targets that need a renderer, which [`dev_docs/KEYFRAMER_COVERAGE.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/KEYFRAMER_COVERAGE.md) lists.

## What a scope watches

A scope holds no values of its own. It holds *targets*: places to read from and write to. The
simplest is a uniform `Structure`, and the interesting wrinkle is the `@` in a key name: everything
after the last `@` is the property driven on the target, so a glow pass and a blur pass can both own
a `radius` without colliding.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/keyframer_examples/capture_apply.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" h="620" padding="16"}

val glow = Structure()
val blur = Structure()
glow.bind("radius") { 4.0f }
glow.bind("intensity") { 0.35f }
blur.bind("radius") { 12.0f }

// The part after the last '@' is the property driven on the structure. Both passes have a
// `radius`; the qualifier is what keeps them apart in the key.
scope.target("glow@radius", glow)
scope.target("glow@intensity", glow)
scope.target("blur@radius", blur)

// The snapshot. Reading only — nothing is written anywhere.
val captured = scope.capture()

// Now fiddle, the way you would with the sketch running, and make it so.

Objects that are not shader `Structure`s can join the same system through an explicit getter and
setter. The low-level form remains `target(name, get, set)`, but ordinary locals should use the typed
forms: `floatTarget`, `doubleTarget`, `booleanTarget`, `intTarget`, `vector2Target`,
`vector3Target`, `vector4Target`, or `stringTarget`. Their setters validate the loaded value at the
scope boundary, and the vector forms copy mutable vectors in both directions. A saved key never ends
up aliasing a live local.

Boolean and integer locals become float lanes, which is what gives them meaningful interpolation:
a Boolean crosses at `0.5`, while an integer rounds and optionally clamps on apply. That suits
controls such as an instance count, which changes CPU-authored geometry but should still travel
smoothly between two looks.

var layers = 3

    floatTarget("outlines.opacity", { opacity }) { opacity = it }
    intTarget("outlines.layers", { layers }, 0..64) { layers = it }
}
```

### One value shared by a local, a control and a key

A normal `controlGroup` control caches its own visible value, while a keyframe normally drives a
Kotlin local. Registering those independently creates two authorities: recalling a key moves the
picture but leaves the slider behind, and rerunning the box can then restore that stale slider over
the recalled value.

The `keyframe*` control helpers make the local authoritative and the UI its writable mirror. A hand
moving the control writes the local. A key applying a value writes the same local and moves both the
desktop control and the remote controller. The programmatic UI update refreshes the box's live rerun
cache but does not emit one document operation per animation frame.

underlying grouped controls also hand back a `ControlValueHandle<T>`; `handle.set(value)` is the
UI-only half of that, for a custom integration that needs it. It never invokes the control callback,
so it cannot start a feedback loop.

### A custom class contributes lanes instead of inventing a file format

A score, instrument or simulation can implement `KeyframeContributor`. Its job is only to register
stable names and live getters/setters. `include` adds those lanes to an existing scope, alongside
shader structures, locals and controls; the ordinary `Key` JSON remains the sole persistence format.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
class Look : KeyframeContributor {
    var opacity = 1f
    var position = vec(0, 0, 0)

    override fun registerKeyframes(scope: KeyframeScope, prefix: String) = with(scope) {
        floatTarget("$prefix.opacity", { opacity }) { opacity = it }
        vector3Target("$prefix.position", { position }) { position = it }
    }
}

val keys = KeyframeScope(schemaVersion = 2).include(Look(), prefix = "foreground")
```

Composition-specific choices stay in the contributor: what a lane means, when its setter is queued,
whether a zero retires a resource, and how the names are versioned. Field only supplies composition,
typed boundaries, interpolation and persistence.

Besides a `Structure`, a scope can target a member of a live module's uniform block:
`target(module, "key@block.member")`, with `ComputeModulePointer` and `MeshModulePointer` forms. These
need a live renderer, so every fence on this page uses the plain `Structure` form.

??? aside "`capture()` reads and writes back either kind of property"

    A `Structure` can hold a property two ways: `structure.bind("radius") { 4f }` installs a
    binding, and `structure["radius"] = 4f` stores a value (and removes any binding). `capture()`
    reads binding-first-then-value (`keyframer.kt:572#private fun readProperty(structure: Structure?, property: String): Any? {`), the same precedence `Structure.get`
    (`Structure.kt:188#operator fun <T> get(property: String) =`) and the buffer writer (`Structure.kt:360`) use. Either kind snapshots,
    including a child `Structure`, whose bindings live in the *root's* map under a dotted path.

    Applying a key writes each property back the kind it was: a value as a value, a binding as a
    binding.

## A camera move is a screw motion, not a straight line

`KeyframeScope.camera` registers a `Camera` as a target. What it stores is not a position and a
target point but a `CameraPose`: the camera's rigid transform as a dual quaternion, plus the focus
distance. That choice is what makes the target worth having, and the difference is easiest to see
drawn.

Interpolating a dual quaternion is a *screw motion* (`CameraPose.sclerp`, `CameraPose.kt:45#fun sclerp(other: CameraPose, t: Float): CameraPose =`, over
`DualQuaternionf.sclerp`, `DualQuaternionf.kt:158#fun sclerp(other: DualQuaternionf, t: Float, dest:`): a rotation and a translation about one axis,
performed together. Interpolating a position is a straight line. Between two cameras that both look
at the same subject, those are very different moves:

**`missingKey` is how a scope outgrows its own files.** Version 0 was written before `wet` existed;
loading it into a scope that declares `missingKey("wet", 0.5f)` fills the gap. The schema-qualified
form, `missingKey(1, "mode", …)`, applies only to files stamped with that `schemaVersion`, and it
is applied *after* the version-agnostic defaults — for a matching file it wins. Nothing ever
*rejects* a file for having a different schema version; the stamp only selects defaults.

**A name present in the file always beats a default**, even when its value is null.

`gain` was saved as the `Float` `0.20f` and appears on disk as `0.20000000298023224`, because every
number goes over the wire as a `Double`. The round trip is still exact: `"kind": "FLOAT"` is carried
alongside, and `KValue.toAny` uses it to narrow the value back to a `Float`, recovering `0.2f`
precisely.

A `Long` is stored exactly, as its own `"type": "long"`. A `Number` that is none of the six kinds,
such as a `BigDecimal`, is stored as a `DOUBLE` and comes back a `Double`.

### Version history on disk

`<file>.versions` holds one numbered JSON file per save, plus a `manifest.json` carrying the two
things a file name cannot: each version's note and its timestamp. The two can disagree. A manifest
can be truncated by a crash mid-write, hand-edited, cut short by a full disk, or half-synced, and
`saveKey` writes the numbered file *before* the manifest row, leaving a window in which a file
exists that no row mentions.

The numbered files win. Because `keyVersions` returns the union of the two, neither alone can lose a
version:

- A **file no row mentions** is listed anyway, with the file's own modification time and a note
  reading `(recovered from disk; the manifest row for this version was lost)`. That marker shows up
  in the history table, saying that the snapshot survived and its note did not.
- A **row whose file is gone** is still listed, because the row is the only surviving evidence that
  the version existed. Loading it throws rather than returning something else.
- `saveKey` takes its next number from that union, so it never reuses an index and never overwrites
  an existing snapshot. That is the same way `nextSafeSaveBackup`
  (`saving.kt:1906#private fun File.nextSafeSaveBackup(backupDir: File): File {`) numbers a document backup: off the directory listing rather than off a
  side file.

An unreadable manifest is reported on the `error,keyframer` log channel rather than swallowed, and
the next `saveKey` moves it aside to `manifest.json.corrupt` instead of overwriting it. The notes in
a half-written file are still there for you to read.

## A captured look becomes source

The last step of the loop closes it. `Key.updateCode()` emits the snapshot as pasteable Kotlin: an
`update { … }` or `updateAndApply { … }` block, sorted by name, so that a state you arrived at by
fiddling becomes a diff you can commit.

        // have let the '$' interpolate at paste time; it now falls back to an escaped literal.
        "block" to SourceBackedBlock<Any?>("box-1", "val total = 2\nprintln(\"sum: \$total\")"),
        "notes" to listOf<String>("unsupported", "on purpose"), // typed: a bare [..] has no element type here
    ),

:::fold render the generated update code

${key.updateCode("look")}

![The emitted Kotlin: look.updateAndApply with assignments sorted by name, showing an escaped source-block string with a backslash before its dollar, gain as 0.65f, a fully-qualified Quaternionf constructor, seed as 99L, and the unsupported list emitted as null behind a block comment](assets/keyframer_examples/update_code.png)

Every literal is chosen so the paste round-trips as the same *type*, not merely the same number.
`0.65f` keeps its `f`, because without it a captured `Float` comes back as a `Double` literal and
`Key.set` does not re-coerce numbers. `99L` keeps its `L`; bytes and shorts get
`.toByte()` / `.toShort()`. Vectors come out as `vec(…)`, quaternions and poses as fully-qualified
constructor calls, and StackSL as `stackSLString(…)` so it stays *code* rather than decaying to a
string. A value outside that set (the list here) becomes `null` behind an `/* unsupported */`
comment: the emitted code still compiles, and nulls that one value.

The escaped `\$` in the source block is `kotlinRawStringLiteral` declining a raw string.
It reaches for one unless the body contains `"""`, ends in a quote, or contains a `$`. That last
case matters: a raw string still interpolates `$name` and `${…}`, and a block mentioning either
would paste as code that failed to compile or that silently substituted something else,
defeating the exact round trip `updateCode` exists for. Those bodies get the escaped literal
instead.

`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard()` is the same string, put on the system clipboard. That one goes
through AWT and replaces whatever the user had copied; on a headless JVM it logs a warning and
only returns the string.

## Blending two programs, not just two numbers

A key can hold a `stack.auto` slot's *numbers* without its code: `stackAutoNumbers(module, name)` registers
one lane per number, which a key turns on the GPU with no recompile (see [its numbers,
live](stacksl_examples.md#its-numbers-live)).

A key can hold code — a `stack.auto` StackSL program registered with `stackAuto`, or a Kotlin
expression captured by the `sourceBlock { }` macro. By default `interpolate` **steps** those: the
left source until `t` reaches 1, then the right one. There is no midpoint between two arbitrary
programs, and a program assembled out of halves of two others is not one either.

Two programs that differ only in *numbers* are the exception, and they are the common case when the
two keys are two looks for one patch. `codeBlend` turns that case on:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val warm = "uv 3.0 * fbm 0.15 + [1.0,0.55,0.2] *"
val cool = "uv 8.0 * fbm 0.45 + [0.2,0.5,1.0] *"

val plan = planStackSLCodeBlend(warm, cool, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME))
println(
    plan.describe(),
)

/*
 stacksl blend: 3 moving site(s) of 3, 0 divergence(s) — RUNTIME -> RUNTIME
   number: 3.0 -> 8.0
   number: 0.15 -> 0.45
   vector: [1.0,0.55,0.2] -> [0.2,0.5,1.0]
 */
```

Both sources are lexed with the language's own tokeniser, the two token streams are aligned on a
longest common subsequence, and a position where the alignment pairs a number with a number becomes
a **site**. A position it cannot pair is a **divergence**, and one divergence puts the whole slot
back on the stepping path. `fbm` against `noise` is a divergence; `3.0` against `8.0` is a site.

Everything outside a site is copied through byte for byte, so a blended program keeps the left one's
comments and layout.

### STATIC and RUNTIME

`CodeBlendMode.STATIC` writes the interpolated numbers into the source: `uv 3.0 * fbm` and
`uv 8.0 * fbm` become `uv 5.5 * fbm` at `t = 0.5`. It reaches every numeric position, and it costs a
compile for every value of `t`. Use it to scrub or to step between looks.

`CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME` emits one program that reads the blend from outside, so it compiles once and
animates for nothing. Each moving literal becomes a push of both endpoints and the builtin `mix`:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
uv 3.0 8.0 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix * fbm 0.15 0.45 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix + …
```

`mix` leaves one value on the stack exactly as the literal it replaced did, so the surrounding stack
arithmetic is untouched. Two StackSL forms cannot be rewritten this way, because their grammar wants
a literal in that position: a modifier chain (`0.35s3`) and a random range (`0.2_0.5`). A plan
containing one reports `runtimeCapable = false`, and a RUNTIME request comes back as
`effectiveMode == STATIC` with `downgradeReason` saying why.

### The push-constant convention

A `stack.auto` slot cannot declare a uniform of its own, so the blend parameter arrives by
agreement: a `vec4` called `keyframeBlend` in the shader's push-constant block, and a keyframe lane
of the same name for the scope to write.

```diffstatic {data-lang=glsl}
layout(push_constant) uniform Controls {
    vec4 keyframeBlend;
} pc;
```

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
scope.target("keyframeBlend") { module.current.liveUniformStructures["pc"] }
scope.codeBlend = CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)
```

`interpolate` fills that lane with `keyframeBlendVector(t)` on every blend, and only when a target of
that name is registered. The four components are the same `t` in four shapes — `x` raw and
unclamped, `y` clamped, `z` smoothstepped, `w` the complement of `y` — so a program can read a
different one per number by setting `CodeBlendOptions.lane`. A block instance called something other
than `pc` is handled by `stackSLRead`.

Kotlin has the same two modes and a different transport. Generated source cannot close over a Kotlin
value, so a moving literal becomes a call that reads the parameter out of a registry slot addressed
by an integer written into the text:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
gain * afield.animation.keyframes.kfMix(0.5f, 1.5f, afield.animation.keyframes.keyframeBlendAmount(7, 0))
```

Fully qualified, so it resolves inside a `sourceBlock` body in a box that imported nothing. One
thing to know before you call the result: a blended block compiles its generated source in the box
the two keyframes came from, so invoke it from a frame loop, a control callback or another box — not
from inside that box's own running code, which stops with an error saying so. The whole call is handed the endpoints
rather than their components, which is what lets a `Quaternionf`
site slerp and a `DualQuaternionf` site sclerp instead of drifting through the inside of the sphere
component by component. A literal keeps its type: `0.5f` and `1.5f` blend to a `Float`, `1` and `3`
to an `Int`, and a hexadecimal or unsigned literal is left alone.

### Seeing what it decided

A blend that stepped looks exactly like a blend that is not working, so the plan is the thing to
read. `plan.describe()` is the text above; `display(plan)` renders the same breakdown as a table of
sites with each one's midpoint. `scope.codeBlendPlans(a, b)` returns a plan per code slot for a pair
of keys, and the [keyframe collection browser](#browsing-saved-keys)'s **Code blend** button does that for the
two keys you have selected there.

[`keyframe_code_blend`](agent_transcripts.md#keyframe_code_blend) blends two looks, renders the

# Keyframes: capturing, persisting and replaying live state

*Every `keyframer.kt` declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference:
[`keyframer.kt`](reference/graphics.md#keyframer-kt). The two supporting types the examples lean on,
`afield.graphics.vulkan.buffers.Structure` and `afield.graphics.vulkan.util.CameraPose`, are not: they live in
Field 4, which the [reference](reference/index.md) leaves to
[Field 4 Graphics](afield_four_graphics.md).*

Live coding has a specific kind of loss built into it. You push sliders around for twenty minutes,
arrive somewhere good, and then the thing you arrived at exists only as the current contents of a
running process. Reload the shader and it is gone. Close the document and it is gone. Try to
reproduce it tomorrow from memory and you get something that is *nearly* it, which is worse.

`keyframer.kt` is the answer to that: a `KeyframeScope` is a set of named live targets, `capture()`
reads all of them into a `Key`, and invoking that `Key` writes them all back. Once a look is a
`Key`, it is an ordinary value: you can diff it against another one, blend between them, write it
to disk with a version history, or turn it into Kotlin source you can paste into a box and commit.

The blending half of this (numbers and vectors easing while *code* steps discretely) has a worked
example over on
[Values over time](interpolants_examples.md#keyframes-morphing-a-whole-parameter-state-including-code).
This page is the rest of it: what a scope can watch, why a camera move is a screw motion, how saving
works and what survives it, and how a captured look becomes source.

Almost everything below runs on the CPU, without a renderer.

## What a scope watches

A scope holds no values of its own. It holds *targets*: places to read from and write to. The
simplest is a uniform `Structure`, and the interesting wrinkle is the `@` in a key name: everything
after the last `@` is the property driven on the target, so a glow pass and a blur pass can both own
a `radius` without colliding.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/keyframer_examples/capture_apply.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" h="620" padding="16"}

// Two independent uniform structures, as a glow pass and a blur pass would each have.
val glow = Structure()
val blur = Structure()
glow.bind("radius") { 4.0f }
glow.bind("intensity") { 0.35f }
blur.bind("radius") { 12.0f }

val scope = KeyframeScope()
// The part after the last '@' is the property driven on the structure. Both passes have a
// `radius`; the qualifier is what keeps them apart in the key.
scope.target("glow@radius", glow)
scope.target("glow@intensity", glow)
scope.target("blur@radius", blur)

// The snapshot. Reading only — nothing is written anywhere.
val captured = scope.capture()

// Now fiddle, the way you would with the sketch running, and make it so.
val edited = captured.copy().update {
    this["glow@radius"] = 9.0f
    this["glow@intensity"] = 0.80f
}
edited()

// Read the live structures back to prove the write actually landed — and that it landed on the
// bare property name, not on the qualified key name.
fun live(s: Structure, p: String) = s.bindings[p]?.invoke()?.toString() ?: "{dim:unbound}"
// Read now, while the edit is still applied — the next line puts the old values back.
val liveRows =
    [
            "glow.radius" to live(glow, "radius"),
            "glow.intensity" to live(glow, "intensity"),
            "blur.radius" to live(blur, "radius"),
            "glow.*glow@radius*" to live(glow, "glow@radius"),

        .joinToString("\n") { (k, v) -> "| $k | $v |" }

// Put the original back, and diff to show the scope is exactly where it started.
captured()
val restored = scope.capture()

:::fold render the four panels

Objects that are not shader `Structure`s can join the same system through an explicit getter and
setter. The low-level form remains `target(name, get, set)`, but ordinary locals should use the typed
forms: `floatTarget`, `doubleTarget`, `booleanTarget`, `intTarget`, `vector2Target`,
`vector3Target`, `vector4Target`, or `stringTarget`. Their setters validate the loaded value at the
scope boundary, and the vector forms copy mutable vectors in both directions. A saved key never ends
up aliasing a live local.

Boolean and integer locals become float lanes, which is what gives them meaningful interpolation:
a Boolean crosses at `0.5`, while an integer rounds and optionally clamps on apply. That suits
controls such as an instance count, which changes CPU-authored geometry but should still travel
smoothly between two looks.

var layers = 3

val scope = KeyframeScope().apply {
    floatTarget("outlines.opacity", { opacity }) { opacity = it }
    intTarget("outlines.layers", { layers }, 0..64) { layers = it }
}
```

### One value shared by a local, a control and a key

A normal `controlGroup` control caches its own visible value, while a keyframe normally drives a
Kotlin local. Registering those independently creates two authorities: recalling a key moves the
picture but leaves the slider behind, and rerunning the box can then restore that stale slider over
the recalled value.

The `keyframe*` control helpers make the local authoritative and the UI its writable mirror. A hand
moving the control writes the local. A key applying a value writes the same local and moves both the
desktop control and the remote controller. The programmatic UI update refreshes the box's live rerun
cache but does not emit one document operation per animation frame.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
var gain = 0.35f
var projectedOnly = false
val keys = KeyframeScope()

thisBox.controlGroup("projected light") {
    keyframeFloatSlider(
        scope = keys,
        name = "light.gain",
        label = "gain",
        min = 0.0,
        max = 4.0,
        get = { gain },
        set = { gain = it },
    )
    keyframeCheckbox(
        scope = keys,
        name = "light.projectedOnly",
        label = "projected only",
        get = { projectedOnly },
        set = { projectedOnly = it },
    )

```

There are matching helpers for a `Double` slider, vec2 control, colour picker and text input. The
underlying grouped controls also hand back a `ControlValueHandle<T>`; `handle.set(value)` is the
UI-only half of that, for a custom integration that needs it. It never invokes the control callback,
so it cannot start a feedback loop.

### A custom class contributes lanes instead of inventing a file format

A score, instrument or simulation can implement `KeyframeContributor`. Its job is only to register
stable names and live getters/setters. `include` adds those lanes to an existing scope, alongside
shader structures, locals and controls; the ordinary `Key` JSON remains the sole persistence format.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
class Look : KeyframeContributor {
    var opacity = 1f
    var position = vec(0, 0, 0)

    override fun registerKeyframes(scope: KeyframeScope, prefix: String) = with(scope) {
        floatTarget("$prefix.opacity", { opacity }) { opacity = it }
        vector3Target("$prefix.position", { position }) { position = it }
    }
}

val keys = KeyframeScope(schemaVersion = 2).include(Look(), prefix = "foreground")
```

Composition-specific choices stay in the contributor: what a lane means, when its setter is queued,
whether a zero retires a resource, and how the names are versioned. Field only supplies composition,
typed boundaries, interpolation and persistence.

Besides a `Structure`, a scope can target a member of a live module's uniform block:
`target(module, "key@block.member")`, with `ComputeModulePointer` and `MeshModulePointer` forms. These
need a live renderer, so every fence on this page uses the plain `Structure` form.

??? aside "`capture()` reads and writes back either kind of property"

    A `Structure` can hold a property two ways: `structure.bind("radius") { 4f }` installs a
    binding, and `structure["radius"] = 4f` stores a value (and removes any binding). `capture()`
    reads binding-first-then-value (`keyframer.kt:572#private fun readProperty(structure: Structure?, property: String): Any? {`), the same precedence `Structure.get`
    (`Structure.kt:188#operator fun <T> get(property: String) =`) and the buffer writer (`Structure.kt:360`) use. Either kind snapshots,
    including a child `Structure`, whose bindings live in the *root's* map under a dotted path.

    Applying a key writes each property back the kind it was: a value as a value, a binding as a
    binding.

## A camera move is a screw motion, not a straight line

`KeyframeScope.camera` registers a `Camera` as a target. What it stores is not a position and a
target point but a `CameraPose`: the camera's rigid transform as a dual quaternion, plus the focus
distance. That choice is what makes the target worth having, and the difference is easiest to see
drawn.

Interpolating a dual quaternion is a *screw motion* (`CameraPose.sclerp`, `CameraPose.kt:45#fun sclerp(other: CameraPose, t: Float): CameraPose =`, over
`DualQuaternionf.sclerp`, `DualQuaternionf.kt:158#fun sclerp(other: DualQuaternionf, t: Float, dest:`): a rotation and a translation about one axis,
performed together. Interpolating a position is a straight line. Between two cameras that both look
at the same subject, those are very different moves:

## Saving: every save is history

`saveKey` writes pretty JSON, and every single time also appends a numbered copy to a
`<file>.versions` directory with a manifest. Saving is always additive; nothing prunes it.

What survives the trip is a closed set. `KValue.fromAny` recognises numbers, Booleans,
`vec2`/`3`/`4`, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed
block. Anything else (a list, a null) is left out, and each one is reported on the
`error,keyframer` log channel.

![Four panels: a three-row version history numbered 0 to 2 with notes; a line reading kept enabled and gain, and left out absent and taps; a reloaded key showing gain, pos, voice plus the filled-in wet and mode defaults; and the pretty-printed JSON of version zero](assets/keyframer_examples/persistence.png)

**`missingKey` is how a scope outgrows its own files.** Version 0 was written before `wet` existed;
loading it into a scope that declares `missingKey("wet", 0.5f)` fills the gap. The schema-qualified
form, `missingKey(1, "mode", …)`, applies only to files stamped with that `schemaVersion`, and it
is applied *after* the version-agnostic defaults — for a matching file it wins. Nothing ever
*rejects* a file for having a different schema version; the stamp only selects defaults.

**A name present in the file always beats a default**, even when its value is null.

`gain` was saved as the `Float` `0.20f` and appears on disk as `0.20000000298023224`, because every
number goes over the wire as a `Double`. The round trip is still exact: `"kind": "FLOAT"` is carried
alongside, and `KValue.toAny` uses it to narrow the value back to a `Float`, recovering `0.2f`
precisely.

A `Long` is stored exactly, as its own `"type": "long"`. A `Number` that is none of the six kinds,
such as a `BigDecimal`, is stored as a `DOUBLE` and comes back a `Double`.

### Version history on disk

`<file>.versions` holds one numbered JSON file per save, plus a `manifest.json` carrying the two
things a file name cannot: each version's note and its timestamp. The two can disagree. A manifest
can be truncated by a crash mid-write, hand-edited, cut short by a full disk, or half-synced, and
`saveKey` writes the numbered file *before* the manifest row, leaving a window in which a file
exists that no row mentions.

The numbered files win. Because `keyVersions` returns the union of the two, neither alone can lose a
version:

- A **file no row mentions** is listed anyway, with the file's own modification time and a note
  reading `(recovered from disk; the manifest row for this version was lost)`. That marker shows up
  in the history table, saying that the snapshot survived and its note did not.
- A **row whose file is gone** is still listed, because the row is the only surviving evidence that
  the version existed. Loading it throws rather than returning something else.
- `saveKey` takes its next number from that union, so it never reuses an index and never overwrites
  an existing snapshot. That is the same way `nextSafeSaveBackup`
  (`saving.kt:1906#private fun File.nextSafeSaveBackup(backupDir: File): File {`) numbers a document backup: off the directory listing rather than off a
  side file.

An unreadable manifest is reported on the `error,keyframer` log channel rather than swallowed, and
the next `saveKey` moves it aside to `manifest.json.corrupt` instead of overwriting it. The notes in
a half-written file are still there for you to read.

### Browsing saved keys

A directory of saved keys is easier to read laid out than listed. `keyframeBrowser(dir, scope = …)`
puts the keyframe collection browser in a box's output: every key in the directory, every slot any
of them holds, and each slot's saved values plotted across its range, so you can see at a glance
which slots the looks actually disagree about. Passing the `scope` is what makes it live: with
it, **Apply** writes a selected key back into the scope's targets, a slot the scope watches but no
key holds shows as never saved, and a slot a key holds that the scope no longer watches is struck
through. Without it the browser only reads.

## A captured look becomes source

The last step of the loop closes it. `Key.updateCode()` emits the snapshot as pasteable Kotlin: an
`update { … }` or `updateAndApply { … }` block, sorted by name, so that a state you arrived at by
fiddling becomes a diff you can commit.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/keyframer_examples/update_code.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" h="560" padding="16"}

val key = scope.Key(

        "steps" to 12,

        "spin" to Quaternionf().setAngleAxis(0.7f, 0f, 1f, 0f),
        "voice" to stackSLString("sin 220 * fold"),
        // A source block whose body mentions a '$'. Emitting this as a Kotlin *raw* string would
        // have let the '$' interpolate at paste time; it now falls back to an escaped literal.
        "block" to SourceBackedBlock<Any?>("box-1", "val total = 2\nprintln(\"sum: \$total\")"),
        "notes" to listOf<String>("unsupported", "on purpose"), // typed: a bare [..] has no element type here
    ),

:::fold render the generated update code
// A multi-line value goes into a fence at column zero, so it arrives byte for byte.

${key.updateCode("look")}

![The emitted Kotlin: look.updateAndApply with assignments sorted by name, showing an escaped source-block string with a backslash before its dollar, gain as 0.65f, a fully-qualified Quaternionf constructor, seed as 99L, and the unsupported list emitted as null behind a block comment](assets/keyframer_examples/update_code.png)

Every literal is chosen so the paste round-trips as the same *type*, not merely the same number.
`0.65f` keeps its `f`, because without it a captured `Float` comes back as a `Double` literal and
`Key.set` does not re-coerce numbers. `99L` keeps its `L`; bytes and shorts get
`.toByte()` / `.toShort()`. Vectors come out as `vec(…)`, quaternions and poses as fully-qualified
constructor calls, and StackSL as `stackSLString(…)` so it stays *code* rather than decaying to a
string. A value outside that set (the list here) becomes `null` behind an `/* unsupported */`
comment: the emitted code still compiles, and nulls that one value.

The escaped `\$` in the source block is `kotlinRawStringLiteral` declining a raw string.
It reaches for one unless the body contains `"""`, ends in a quote, or contains a `$`. That last
case matters: a raw string still interpolates `$name` and `${…}`, and a block mentioning either
would paste as code that failed to compile or that silently substituted something else,
defeating the exact round trip `updateCode` exists for. Those bodies get the escaped literal
instead.

`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard()` is the same string, put on the system clipboard. That one goes
through AWT and replaces whatever the user had copied; on a headless JVM it logs a warning and
only returns the string.

## Blending two programs, not just two numbers

A key can hold a `stack.auto` slot's *numbers* without its code: `stackAutoNumbers(module, name)` registers
one lane per number, which a key turns on the GPU with no recompile (see [its numbers,
live](stacksl_examples.md#its-numbers-live)).

A key can hold code — a `stack.auto` StackSL program registered with `stackAuto`, or a Kotlin
expression captured by the `sourceBlock { }` macro. By default `interpolate` **steps** those: the
left source until `t` reaches 1, then the right one. There is no midpoint between two arbitrary
programs, and a program assembled out of halves of two others is not one either.

Two programs that differ only in *numbers* are the exception, and they are the common case when the
two keys are two looks for one patch. `codeBlend` turns that case on:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val warm = "uv 3.0 * fbm 0.15 + [1.0,0.55,0.2] *"
val cool = "uv 8.0 * fbm 0.45 + [0.2,0.5,1.0] *"

val plan = planStackSLCodeBlend(warm, cool, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME))
println(
    plan.describe(),
)

/*
 stacksl blend: 3 moving site(s) of 3, 0 divergence(s) — RUNTIME -> RUNTIME
   number: 3.0 -> 8.0
   number: 0.15 -> 0.45
   vector: [1.0,0.55,0.2] -> [0.2,0.5,1.0]
 */
```

Both sources are lexed with the language's own tokeniser, the two token streams are aligned on a
longest common subsequence, and a position where the alignment pairs a number with a number becomes
a **site**. A position it cannot pair is a **divergence**, and one divergence puts the whole slot
back on the stepping path. `fbm` against `noise` is a divergence; `3.0` against `8.0` is a site.

Everything outside a site is copied through byte for byte, so a blended program keeps the left one's
comments and layout.

### STATIC and RUNTIME

`CodeBlendMode.STATIC` writes the interpolated numbers into the source: `uv 3.0 * fbm` and
`uv 8.0 * fbm` become `uv 5.5 * fbm` at `t = 0.5`. It reaches every numeric position, and it costs a
compile for every value of `t`. Use it to scrub or to step between looks.

`CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME` emits one program that reads the blend from outside, so it compiles once and
animates for nothing. Each moving literal becomes a push of both endpoints and the builtin `mix`:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
uv 3.0 8.0 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix * fbm 0.15 0.45 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix + …
```

`mix` leaves one value on the stack exactly as the literal it replaced did, so the surrounding stack
arithmetic is untouched. Two StackSL forms cannot be rewritten this way, because their grammar wants
a literal in that position: a modifier chain (`0.35s3`) and a random range (`0.2_0.5`). A plan
containing one reports `runtimeCapable = false`, and a RUNTIME request comes back as
`effectiveMode == STATIC` with `downgradeReason` saying why.

### The push-constant convention

A `stack.auto` slot cannot declare a uniform of its own, so the blend parameter arrives by
agreement: a `vec4` called `keyframeBlend` in the shader's push-constant block, and a keyframe lane
of the same name for the scope to write.

```diffstatic {data-lang=glsl}
layout(push_constant) uniform Controls {
    vec4 keyframeBlend;
} pc;
```

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
scope.target("keyframeBlend") { module.current.liveUniformStructures["pc"] }
scope.codeBlend = CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)
```

`interpolate` fills that lane with `keyframeBlendVector(t)` on every blend, and only when a target of
that name is registered. The four components are the same `t` in four shapes — `x` raw and
unclamped, `y` clamped, `z` smoothstepped, `w` the complement of `y` — so a program can read a
different one per number by setting `CodeBlendOptions.lane`. A block instance called something other
than `pc` is handled by `stackSLRead`.

Kotlin has the same two modes and a different transport. Generated source cannot close over a Kotlin
value, so a moving literal becomes a call that reads the parameter out of a registry slot addressed
by an integer written into the text:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
gain * afield.animation.keyframes.kfMix(0.5f, 1.5f, afield.animation.keyframes.keyframeBlendAmount(7, 0))
```

Fully qualified, so it resolves inside a `sourceBlock` body in a box that imported nothing. One
thing to know before you call the result: a blended block compiles its generated source in the box
the two keyframes came from, so invoke it from a frame loop, a control callback or another box — not
from inside that box's own running code, which stops with an error saying so. The whole call is handed the endpoints
rather than their components, which is what lets a `Quaternionf`
site slerp and a `DualQuaternionf` site sclerp instead of drifting through the inside of the sphere
component by component. A literal keeps its type: `0.5f` and `1.5f` blend to a `Float`, `1` and `3`
to an `Int`, and a hexadecimal or unsigned literal is left alone.

### Seeing what it decided

A blend that stepped looks exactly like a blend that is not working, so the plan is the thing to
read. `plan.describe()` is the text above; `display(plan)` renders the same breakdown as a table of
sites with each one's midpoint. `scope.codeBlendPlans(a, b)` returns a plan per code slot for a pair
of keys, and the [keyframe collection browser](#browsing-saved-keys)'s **Code blend** button does that for the
two keys you have selected there.

The whole feature is a runnable starting point:
[`keyframe_code_blend`](agent_transcripts.md#keyframe_code_blend) blends two looks, renders the
runtime program at five values of the push constant, and compares both ends against the keyframe they are supposed to be.
